subject: Science
central_question: How can mixtures be classified and their components separated by using differences in properties such as particle size, solubility, density, boiling point and movement through a medium?
in_scope_units: 5.1 How Can We Classify Mixtures? — homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures, supported by observations of salt water, chalk water and milk water in Activity 5.1
5.2 Solutions — solute, solvent and the homogeneous nature of a solution
5.2.1 Concentration of a solution — the importance of the correct proportion of solute and solvent
5.2.2 How do we express concentration? — mass by mass, mass by volume and volume by volume percentages
5.2.3 Solubility of substances — solubility, saturated solutions, temperature dependence and solubility curves
5.3 Methods of Separation of Homogeneous Mixtures — choosing methods by using differences in solubility, boiling point and movement through paper
5.3.1 Crystallization — obtaining or purifying a solid from a saturated solution
5.3.2 Distillation — recovering a liquid or separating miscible liquids with sufficiently different boiling points
5.3.3 Paper Chromatography — separating components that move at different rates with a solvent on paper
5.4 How Can We Separate the Components of Heterogeneous Mixtures? — selecting methods according to density, state, particle size and other physical properties
5.4.1 Separation of two immiscible liquids — using a separating funnel and density difference
5.4.2 Sublimation — separating a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable solid and understanding deposition
5.4.3 Suspensions — visible particles, settling, filtration, centrifugation and coagulation
5.4.4 Colloids — particle size, non-settling behaviour and comparison with solutions and suspensions
5.5 Tyndall Effect — scattering of light by colloids and suspensions, dispersed phase, dispersion medium and emulsions
banned_topics: Molarity, molality, normality and mole-fraction calculations
Advanced chromatography calculations such as Rf values
Detailed chemical bonding or atomic structure of mixture components
Balancing chemical equations or teaching reaction mechanisms
Detailed industrial design of petroleum refineries beyond the chapter's brief introduction to fractional distillation
Medical diagnosis procedures beyond the chapter's discussion of centrifugation, paperfuge and blood components

known_pitfalls.claim: Every mixture that looks uniform is a true solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: A colloid such as milk may appear uniform, but it is not a true solution; its particles are larger than solution particles and scatter light.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mass of the solvent alone is used as the denominator in mass by mass percentage.
known_pitfalls.correction: Mass by mass percentage is mass of solute divided by total mass of solution, multiplied by 100.

known_pitfalls.claim: A 5% m/v solution means 5 g of solute in 100 mL of solvent.
known_pitfalls.correction: It means 5 g of solute in 100 mL of the final solution.
The solubility of solid solutes in liquid solvents generally increases with temperature, while the solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature rises.

known_pitfalls.claim: Evaporation, crystallization and distillation are the same process.
known_pitfalls.correction: Evaporation removes a solvent to obtain a solute, crystallization forms purer crystals from a saturated solution, and distillation vaporises and condenses a liquid so that the liquid can be recovered.

known_pitfalls.claim: Distillation can separate any two miscible liquids.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter uses ordinary distillation when the boiling points differ by at least about 25 °C; liquids with smaller differences require fractional distillation.

known_pitfalls.claim: The solvent level in paper chromatography should cover the sample spot.
known_pitfalls.correction: The solvent level must begin below the sample spot so that the rising solvent carries the components up the paper.

known_pitfalls.claim: A separating funnel is used for miscible liquids.
known_pitfalls.correction: A separating funnel is used for immiscible liquids that form layers, and separation depends on their density difference.

known_pitfalls.claim: Sublimation and evaporation both describe a liquid changing into vapour.
known_pitfalls.correction: In sublimation, a solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state; evaporation begins from a liquid.

known_pitfalls.claim: Colloidal particles settle on standing just like suspension particles.
known_pitfalls.correction: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle over time, whereas suspension particles can settle.

known_pitfalls.claim: Solutions show the Tyndall effect because their particles are large.
known_pitfalls.correction: Transparent solutions do not show the Tyndall effect; colloids and suspensions scatter light because their particles are larger.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Activity 5.1 to compare salt water, chalk powder in water and milk in water by visibility, settling, filtration and light scattering.
Use NCERT Examples 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 in sequence to practise % m/m, % m/v and % v/v concentration.
Use NCERT Activity 5.2 and Fig. 5.6 to read a solubility curve and predict the effect of cooling a saturated solution.
Use NCERT Activity 5.3 to explain the complete crystallization procedure and why slow cooling gives larger, well-shaped crystals.
Use the acetone-water case in NCERT Section 5.3.2 and Revise, Reflect, Refine Q12 to connect boiling-point difference with distillation.
Use NCERT Activity 5.5 to explain why the solvent level must remain below the ink spot in paper chromatography.
Use NCERT Activities 5.6 and 5.7 to contrast separation by density in a separating funnel with separation by sublimation.
Use NCERT Activities 5.8 and 5.9 together with Revise, Reflect, Refine Q2, Q3, Q6 and Q10 to compare suspensions, colloids, centrifugation, coagulation and the Tyndall effect.
Finish with NCERT Revise, Reflect, Refine Q13 and Q14 for data-based solubility and concentration calculations, and Q15 for identification of a distillation set-up.
